1.pericope_label: Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, unto the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints which are in all Achaia: Grace be to you and peace from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

schools.summary: Do the prosopography and the geography: Timothy replaces Sosthenes and is no co-author, perhaps an amanuensis, and Achaia means the whole Roman province, wide enough to take in Cenchreae; give three motives for naming him, that he was lately among them, that his authority needed building as a probable successor, and that his testimony could rebut the charge of insincerity about the changed visit.

State the rule that makes the title mean anything: authority requires both a call and fidelity in executing the office, and since the false apostles usurp the title too, he who gives himself out as an apostle must show himself such by his work; then press what the address concedes, that a church existed at Corinth amid such a conflux of evils, since the faults of individuals do not unmake a society that has genuine marks of religion.

Turn the question of occasion into a chronology, dating the letter a year after the former from the notice that Achaia was ready a year ago, and rehearsing Whitby's four arguments for a date after the second entry into Macedonia; then report Titus's news, that the first epistle had overwhelmed them with distress and moved them to excommunicate the offender.

Ask first why a second letter exists at all, and answer twice over: the promised visit was delayed by the Spirit's detaining him in matters of greater necessity, and the Corinthians had amended under the first letter, so that praise was now owing where rebuke had been — which is why the severity is confined to a few places near the end.

Take the epistle as a whole before glossing the parts: a year between the letters, many showing marks of repentance while others still follow the false teachers, and the delayed visit — undertaken out of unwillingness to be severe — turned against him as levity and change of conduct.

debates.question: Why was a second letter written?

sides.position: Because the promised visit was delayed by the Spirit, and because the Corinthians had amended under the first letter and now deserved commendation
Because Titus reported that the first letter had produced distress, self-examination and the excommunication of the offender
Because many had repented while others still followed the false teachers, and the delayed visit had been turned into a charge of levity

outliers.note: Alone dates the epistle by argument, rehearsing Whitby’s four grounds for placing it after the second entry into Macedonia and appealing to the postscript that puts the writing at Philippi.
Alone notes the usage by which Paul, writing to Timothy, calls him his son, but writing of him calls him his brother.

themes: apostle by the will of God

3.pericope_label: Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.

schools.summary: Mark that this is a benediction and not a thanksgiving, an utterance of more exulting joy than the openings of other letters and grounded in God rather than in the readers; weigh whether the second title is a Hebraism for an adjective or means literally that God originates all mercies; and supply the philology of the third, a noun built on a verb meaning to call to one's side, the very word used of the Spirit as Comforter, counted twelve times in this epistle.

Give the opening three purposes at once — to extol God's goodness, to animate the readers by example, and to glory piously against the slanders of the false apostles, since the world derides martyrdoms it ought to admire; add the condition governing every title, that where Christ is not, the beneficence of God is not; and make the comfort a trust to be passed on, chiefly by ministers of the Word.

Say in a line what others take a paragraph to say — the source whence all mercy flows, whether of body or soul, time or eternity; state the relation between mercy and comfort exactly, the one being the fountain and the other its outward expression; and turn the doctrine into an indictment of the preacher who has all his divinity by study and nothing by experience.

Distinguish the senses in which God is Father of Christ — of his divine nature by eternal generation, of his human by the conception in the virgin, and of Christ as God-man and Redeemer by covenant-relation — and set that bond beside the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

debates.question: Is “Father of mercies” a Hebraism or a statement of origin?

sides.position: Possibly a Hebraism standing for an adjective, as in the merciful Father of Jewish prayers, but better taken literally: God originates all mercies
The source whence all mercy flows, whether of body or soul, time or eternity

outliers.note: Alone brings in the recurring formula of the Koran beside the Jewish prayers as a parallel to “the merciful Father”, and alone quotes Sophocles and Virgil on comforting others out of one’s own sorrow before marking where the pagan poets stop short.

The catena carries a catechetical section here arguing about the blinding of unbelievers’ thoughts, which belongs to the fourth chapter of this epistle and never touches this verse; it is set aside. It cannot be declared under excluded_voices because the validator matches the label “Cyril:” while the source writes “Cyril of Jerusalem:”.

5.pericope_label: For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth by Christ. And whether we be afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, which is effectual in the enduring of the same sufferings which we also suffer: or whether we be comforted, it is for your consolation and salvation. And our hope of you is stedfast, knowing, that as ye are partakers of the sufferings, so shall ye be also of the consolation.

schools.summary: Parse the genitive as subjective and let the sufferings overflow, so that partnership in suffering brings partnership in glory; press the union until the sufferings are Christ's own, passing from him to every member of his body that they too may drink his cup; and distinguish the inward and outward sides of the result, since deliverance is seen not in escaping sufferings but in enduring them.

Distinguish the miseries common to good and bad alike — in the wicked tokens of the curse, showing only anger and participation with Adam — from the afflictions in which believers are conformed to Christ; read the clause passively, that God multiplied consolations by the measure of tribulations, as David acknowledged; and report the ancient copies that move the clause about hope into the middle.

Argue the proportion and then illustrate it: because consolation was always matched to the trial they stood as firmly in the heaviest as in the lightest, so a man upheld in a slight trial need not fear a great one — is it not as easy for a man to lift a hundred pounds as for an infant to lift a few ounces? Note also the strange variation in the manuscripts, and point the reader to Griesbach.

Turn the affliction into the readers' comfort without softening it: had we not been afflicted, this had been the ruin of you all; and then, so as not to bring the encomium round to Paul alone, observe that men falling so far short of him are raised to the same dignity of endurance.
Keep to the upshot for the readers, that their faith should not be weakened by what they see in their teachers but their consolations increased.

debates.question: Whose sufferings are “the sufferings of Christ”?

sides.position: Not what Christ endured in his own person in the room and stead of his people, but what he suffers in his members
Sufferings substantially the same in nature as his, arising from opposition, contempt, persecution and want
His own sufferings on earth, passing from him to every member of his body in his mysterious union with the Church
The afflictions in which believers are conformed to Christ, as distinct from the miseries common to good and bad alike

debates.question: What is the true order of the clauses in these verses?

sides.position: The manuscripts vary strangely; the transposed order is to be preferred, on the evidence collected by Griesbach
Some of the most ancient copies place the clause about hope in the middle, and the evidence for it is exceedingly strong
The variation hardly affects the sense in any appreciable degree

outliers.note: Alone turns the proportion of comfort to suffering into a physical illustration: is it not as easy for a man to lift a hundred pounds’ weight as for an infant to lift a few ounces?

8.pericope_label: For we would not, brethren, have you ignorant of our trouble which came to us in Asia, that we were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life: But we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead:

schools.summary: Lay out the candidates for the trouble in Asia with their objections and decline to settle it, since we do not know whether it was sickness or peril; dissent from the whole enterprise by arguing that the unlocalised phrase points to bodily illness rather than a riot; and take the rare word for sentence as a decision rendered, or, more boldly, as the medical opinion formed on a diagnosis, which would make recovery a veritable resurrection.

Rule out both a decree of heaven and a magistrate's sentence, making it an opinion in their own breasts so that they looked on themselves as dead men; take the metaphor from porters overloaded and from ships so overladen they may be lost; and refuse Chrysostom's view that Paul needed no such remedy, insisting he was a man of like passions, liable to misdirected confidence and rashness.

Call the original exceedingly emphatic — weighed down beyond what is credible and beyond what natural strength could support — and admit that no part of the recorded history quite justifies the words, so that the event may be a persecution nowhere on record, of which the Corinthians had been told.

debates.question: What was the trouble in Asia?

sides.position: The riot of Demetrius at Ephesus, which most commentators take
Not that, since Paul did not enter the theatre and so ran no risk justifying these words: rather the fighting with beasts
The Jews lying in wait as he was about to go to Macedonia
Some terrible persecution recorded nowhere, of which the Corinthians had been told
Not a peril at all but bodily illness, since the phrase is unlocalised and the language describes collapse rather than danger
Unknown: we cannot tell whether it was sickness or peril

outliers.note: Alone argues from the unlocalised phrase and from the language of collapse that the trouble in Asia was bodily illness rather than any of the perils the others propose.

Alone refuses Chrysostom’s reading that Paul needed no such remedy and set himself forth as a pattern only in appearance, insisting he was a man of like passions, liable to misdirected confidence and rashness.

10.pericope_label: Who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver: in whom we trust that he will yet deliver us; Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf.

schools.summary: Take the adjective as one of quality rather than quantity, so that the sense is a terrible rather than a great death, and read rescue from it as a kind of resurrection; press the perfect tense of the hoping, which implies that the danger of relapse was not past and that life was for Paul a perpetual series of deliverances; and confess frankly that the sentence about many persons is difficult to understand.

Ascribe the deliverance solely to God as its author while allowing the prayers of the saints as helping causes; and make the sequence a rule about assurance, since the Lord, by accomplishing in part what he promised, bids us hope well for what remains, confirming his promises by as many pledges as we have received favours.

State the ground of confidence in a line, that the circumstances were such that no human power could avail and the interposition was signal enough to be relied on hereafter; and set out the exchange in the prayers, that the prayers of many obtain the gift while the thanksgiving of many acknowledges the mercy, since even an apostle felt the prayers of the Church necessary.

debates.question: What does the rare word rendered “sentence” mean?

sides.position: A judicial verdict, perhaps an actual condemnation to the wild beasts
A decision rendered, as always in Josephus, Polybius and the papyri
An opinion formed in their own breasts, neither a decree of heaven nor a magistrate's sentence
A half-technical medical term for the opinion formed on a diagnosis, or possibly, from a cognate word in Hippocrates, the symptoms of a fatal disease

outliers.note: Alone reads the word for “sentence” as a medical term and offers, from a cognate word frequent in Hippocrates, the alternative that the sense is “we had the symptoms of a fatal disease in us”.
Alone concedes outright that the clause about thanks given by many persons is a difficult sentence to understand, after setting out the options.

12.pericope_label: For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward. For we write none other things unto you, than what ye read or acknowledge; and I trust ye shall acknowledge even to the end; As also ye have acknowledged us in part, that we are your rejoicing, even as ye also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus.

schools.summary: Admit the connexion is not obvious, report how others have joined it to the request for prayer, and prefer the wider context, that a man lately without hope of life found his confidence in having lived holily; note the manuscripts reading holiness for simplicity; and catch the play between reading and knowing fully, asking whether the added preposition means reading between the lines.

Enter the limitation that the glorying is before men and not before God; insist that the compound verb of knowing means more than the simple one, since a man may be silently convinced a thing is true and still not own it; and make the boasting mutual, since it was pious glorying in Paul to have brought them under Christ's obedience and in them to have been trained by such an apostle.

Do the etymology for everyone: simplicity is the not-compounded, having one end in view and no sinister purpose, while sincerity comes from the bright shining of the sun and means such purity as can stand God's light without the discovery of a blemish; then take the verb for conversation as a continual coming back to the point one set out from, acting toward God as the planets toward the sun.

See why the boast stands exactly here: having ascribed all to God's mercies and their prayers, Paul might make the hearer supine, so he shows them something properly their own, a conscience pure and without guile, which avails not merely to comfort but to glorying.

Give the witness its standing — conscience is instead of a thousand witnesses, God's deputy in the soul, and its voice is the voice of God — and let it testify to the constant tenour of a life rather than to this or that single act.

debates.question: Does “in part” mean partly, or some of them?

sides.position: Some of them: a part conceded his uprightness while a faction denied it
The measure of the justice done him, which was real but not adequate
Either may be intended, of the thing known or of the persons knowing

outliers.note: Alone derives the verb rendered “had our conversation” from turning back again and expands it into a figure of circulation, acting toward God as the planets toward the sun, deriving all their light and heat and motion from him.

The catena carries a catechetical section here on the name Ecclesia and the first scriptural use of the word “assemble”, which never touches this verse; it is set aside for the same reason and, like the block at the third verse, cannot be declared under excluded_voices because of the label mismatch.

15.pericope_label: And in this confidence I was minded to come unto you before, that ye might have a second benefit; And to pass by you into Macedonia, and to come again out of Macedonia unto you, and of you to be brought on my way toward Judea.

schools.summary: Reconstruct the original itinerary in full, a voyage from Ephesus to Corinth, then Macedonia, then Corinth again, then Jerusalem, so that the Corinthians were to have two visits and not one; then ask whether the change really showed them less regard, and make much of the verb in the last clause, which expects them to escort him solemnly to the ship and perhaps into Asia.

Make the two benefits the eighteen months of first labour and the confirming visit that was to follow, then turn the disappointment into an accusation, since by their own ingratitude the Corinthians hindered his coming and deprived themselves of the second, paying the penalty of their own fault; and allow, with Chrysostom, that the word may mean joy, while preferring the simpler sense.

Reverse the order others give and put Macedonia first with Corinth on the return, reading the phrase to mean that he would sail up the Aegean leaving Corinth to the west; report the manuscripts that read joy for grace while judging grace the better sense; and make the two benefits the sowing of the seed of life and its watering.

Draw the moral rather than the itinerary: good men should be careful to preserve the reputation of sincerity and constancy, should not resolve except upon mature deliberation, and should not change what they have resolved but for weighty reasons.

debates.question: Which leg of the journey came first in the original plan?

sides.position: Corinth first, then Macedonia, then Corinth again, then Jerusalem
Macedonia first and Corinth on the return, the phrase meaning that he would sail up the Aegean leaving Corinth to the west
Benefit or grace, which expresses the meaning best
Joy, on the reading of Westcott and Hort
Joy, as Chrysostom took it

outliers.note: Alone turns the disappointed visit against the readers, arguing that by their own ingratitude they hindered his coming and so deprived themselves of the second benefit, paying the penalty of their own fault.

17.pericope_label: When I therefore was thus minded, did I use lightness? or the things that I purpose, do I purpose according to the flesh, that with me there should be yea yea, and nay nay? But as God is true, our word toward you was not yea and nay.

schools.summary: Weigh the word for levity as lightness of weight applied to the mind, and read the interrogative as a sharp denial; define purposing after the flesh as forming plans for one's own ease and abandoning them when they prove inconvenient; and ask when the Corinthians can have heard of the plan at all, allowing that either a lost letter or Timothy's commission is possible and no evidence decides.

Ask whether the promise was ever made absolutely, without the condition attached; supply the insinuation being answered, that a man who broke his word about coming was not to be trusted in his ministry either; and observe Paul deliberately transferring the calumny from his person to his doctrine, while admitting it does not follow that a man faithful in doctrine is truthful in everything else.

Put the accusation as two plain questions, whether the purpose was formed without due consideration and whether it was abandoned through fickleness; name the two faults that keep men's purposes from being performed, changing them hourly and forming them rashly, which God punishes by defeating the plans of those who determine as though not subject to his will; and give the reason for the delay, uncertainty about their state.

debates.question: When had the Corinthians heard of the plan Paul defends?

sides.position: Either from a lost letter or from Timothy's commission; no evidence decides between them

debates.question: Where does the yea-yea and nay-nay formula come from?

sides.position: From the rule of the Sermon on the Mount and of James, quoted against Paul with a sneer by a teacher of the circumcision party
From the same two passages, on the evidence of the wording alone
From the ordinary conduct of carnal men who change their purposes as their interest dictates

outliers.note: Alone asks when the Corinthians can have heard of the abandoned plan at all, and alone suggests that the yea-yea formula was quoted against Paul from the Sermon on the Mount by a teacher of the circumcision party — making the passage indirect evidence that the words of the Lord Jesus were cited as rules of life.

19.pericope_label: For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you by us, even by me and Silvanus and Timotheus, was not yea and nay, but in him was yea. For all the promises of God in him are yea, and in him Amen, unto the glory of God by us.

schools.summary: Set out the two reasons for the obligation to veracity, that Christ always showed it and God is always true to his promises, and report the agreement that the doctrine rather than the person is meant; then concede with candour that forensically this is hardly an adequate defence, being an argument of ethical congruity, and report the better manuscripts that read in him is the Yea, wherefore also by him is the Amen.

Ask why Apollos goes unnamed while Silvanus and Timothy are named, and answer that the more a man was assailed by calumniators the more careful Paul was to defend him; insist that the preaching contained nothing but Christ, held forth pure and undisguised rather than presented in a new shape after the manner of Proteus; and rest all the promises on Christ alone, since in no other is the Father propitious to us.

Turn the doctrine back into the argument — had he been a worldly man he must have had the same secular interest in view when he first preached to them — and distribute the two words of the verse, the promise coming originally by Christ and so yea, having its fulfilment through him and so amen, or four ways at once between God promising and men believing, apostles and hearers.

debates.question: Is the appeal to Christ's truthfulness an adequate defence?

sides.position: Not forensically: it is an argument of ethical congruity, resting on the improbability that one who preached the absolutely true Christ should palter with a double sense
It is sufficient, since Paul was bound to veracity both by Christ's example and by God's fidelity to his promises

outliers.note: Alone asks why Apollos goes unmentioned while Silvanus and Timothy are named, and alone uses Proteus for the changeable Christ that Paul refused to preach.
Alone distributes the yea and the amen four ways at once, between God promising and men believing, and between the apostles and their hearers.

21.pericope_label: Now he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is God; Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts.

schools.summary: Trace the whole defence back to God so that nothing looks like boasting, noting who each pronoun covers; render the phrase into Christ rather than in him, as an actual incorporation, and date the anointing to baptism or the laying on of hands; then give the seal its legal weight from the papyri, and trace the word for earnest from Hebrew through Phoenician traders into Greek, Latin, Italian, French and even popular Scotch.

Turn the ratification inward: God always has his Amen, but such is our vanity that we do not utter ours in return except when he testifies surely in our hearts by his Spirit, since to keep pace with God in steadfastness is not in man's power; and catalogue the uses of seals before choosing the certifying sense, the assurance God gives his people of their interest in his love.

Read the anointing of the ministry rather than of believers at large, the miraculous gifts attesting an extraordinary calling and preserving them from dissimulation of every kind; identify the earnest with the pledge Judah gave Tamar and conclude that without it there can be no glory; and mark the distinction English blurs, that a pledge is restored when the debt is paid while an earnest is not taken away but completed.
Put the verse to a use none of the others attempt, citing it among the proofs that Paul and his fellow apostles were full of the Holy Ghost.

debates.question: Who is glorified by the fulfilment of the promises?

sides.position: Christians generally, in whom and through whom the promises are fulfilled
The preacher rather than the hearer, as the context determines
The ministry, by whose instrumentality the promises were fulfilled to them

outliers.note: Alone writes the history of the word for “earnest”, from a Hebrew verb through Phoenician traders to Greece, Carthage and Rome, its shortening in Roman law because the full form was felt vulgar, and its survival into Italian, modern French and popular Scotch.
Alone marks the distinction the English blurs, that a pledge is restored when the debt is paid while an earnest is not taken away but completed.

23.pericope_label: Moreover I call God for a record upon my soul, that to spare you I came not as yet unto Corinth. Not for that we have dominion over your faith, but are helpers of your joy: for by faith ye stand.

schools.summary: Note that the chapter division falls in the wrong place and set out the reconstruction by which the change of purpose was made before the first epistle, Paul choosing to try a letter and let the church discipline the offender itself; correct the rendering to a calling of God to witness against his own soul, and deny that the adverb can mean not yet; then name the closing retraction as a delicate correction of a misapprehension.

Read the oath as an indirect reproach, since it would be unfair that Paul be grieved through their fault and worse that they assent to a calumny putting an innocent man in the place of the guilty; treat the words as a full oath sworn by the living God, the searcher of hearts; and frame the last verse as an objection anticipated — do you then act so tyrannically?

Assemble from the letters themselves the state of Paul's reputation at Corinth, his doctrine opposed and his apostleship questioned; draw from the oath the conclusion that Christ cannot have designed to forbid all swearing, and notice that Paul says elegantly to Corinth rather than to you at the moment he intimates his power to punish; then turn the denial of dominion into a charge against those who claimed the right without the warrant, in a time of thick darkness that might be felt.

Refuse to smooth over the contradiction — above he says he is led everywhere by the Spirit, here that staying away was his own act — and canvass three ways out, preferring the one in which the Spirit forbade at first and Paul afterwards concurred on his own conviction.

debates.question: Did Paul stay away by the Spirit's direction or by his own choice?

sides.position: A contradiction stands here and must be faced: three solutions are possible, and the likeliest is that the Spirit forbade at first and Paul afterwards concurred on his own conviction
By his own choice, made before the first epistle was written, in order to try the effect of a letter first
By his own choice, to give them space to amend before he should be obliged to excommunicate

debates.question: How far may an apostle claim dominion over faith?

sides.position: So far as prescribing articles of belief and forbidding contrary doctrine, which was essential to the office, but never in a lordly manner
Not at all in appearance: the word is a half-apology, since the readers have a standing-ground in their faith independently of him
The disclaimer is entered lest the ministers be thought to assume tyrannical power over the churches

outliers.note: Alone states the contradiction outright — that Paul has just said he is led everywhere by the Spirit and now says the staying away was his own act — and canvasses three solutions rather than choosing the easiest.

Alone uses the oath as an argument that Christ cannot have designed to forbid all swearing, and alone notices that Paul says “to Corinth” rather than “to you” at the moment he intimates his power to punish.

Alone extends the denial of dominion over faith into a polemic against those who claimed the right without apostolic warrant, threatening perdition for doctrines opposed to the letter of Scripture, in a time of thick darkness that might be felt.
